summary:
The search turned up the abstract of the paper you named, which is Barolet's 2009 study in the *Journal of Investigative Dermatology*. I didn't find the full text, so the details below come from abstract excerpts reposted on secondary sites.

**Study design:** The team first tested a 660 nm sequentially pulsed LED on a tissue-engineered human reconstructed skin model, comparing sham and treated samples over 11 sessions. They then ran a split-face, single-blinded study in aged or photoaged people. Histological and biochemical changes were first evaluated in a tissue-engineered Human Reconstructed Skin (HRS) model after 11 sham or LED light treatments. LED effects were then assessed in aged/photoaged individuals in a split-face single-blinded study.

**In vitro results:** Type I procollagen was higher in treated samples and MMP-1 was lower. Results yielded a mean percent difference between LED-treated and non-LED-treated HRS of 31% in levels of type-1 procollagen and of -18% in MMP-1. No histological changes were observed.

**Clinical results:** The abstract reports that more than 90% of individuals showed a reduction in rhytid depth and surface roughness, and, via a blinded clinical assessment, that 87% experienced a reduction in the Fitzpatrick wrinkling severity score after 12 LED treatments. No adverse events or downtime were reported.

**Conclusion:** The authors argue that LED therapy reversed collagen downregulation and MMP-1 upregulation. This could explain the improvements in skin appearance observed in LED-treated individuals.

**Caveats:** The search results don't give sample sizes, control details, or statistical methods for the clinical arm. The in vitro work is a single model, and the clinical claims rest on the authors' own reporting. Several of the search hits came from marketing or clinic websites, so check the original DOI (10.1038/jid.2009.186) for the full methods.
